headline: 史丹頓開放讀者提問
context: 《衛報》開放讀者提問英國演員伊美黛．史丹頓（Imelda Staunton），她演過《王冠》裡的伊麗莎白二世、《哈利波特》系列的恩不里居教授，也是《柏靈頓熊》系列露西阿姨的配音演員。同一天，《衛報》喜劇線記者布萊恩．羅根也公開回覆讀者對愛丁堡藝穗節喜劇評論的提問，包括星級評分制度的爭議。

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.summary: She’s acting royalty – literally, having played Queen Elizabeth II in The Crown – but what questions would you ask her? It is perhaps fitting that Imelda Staunton ended up playing Queen Elizabeth II in the last two series of The Crown, considering she has been acting royalty for years. Her film career has seen her voice champion egg-layer Bunty in 2000’s Chicken Run, followed by roles in Mike Leigh’s 2004 drama Vera Drake and the 2005 comedy Nanny McPhee. In 2014, she played the formidable Welsh miners’ strike campaigner Hefina in Pride . She also plays Lady Maud Bagshaw in the first two Downton Abbey films, and voices Paddington’s beloved Aunt Lucy in all three Paddington films. For a whole generation, however, she will always be Dolores Umbridge in two of the later Harry Potter films, where she somehow made a pink cardigan almost as frightening as Voldemort. On TV, she has cropped up in everything from Little Britain and Doctor Who to Psychoville, Brassic and a memorable guest appearance in the fourth series of A Bit of Fry & Laurie, where – for reasons known only to F&L – she was introduced as “Snutty”. Whether she’s playing a chicken, a bear or the head of state, there is always something unmistakably Imelda about her performances: warm and calm but with the distinct impression that she won’t stand for any nonsense. sources.name: The Guardian
sources.summary: Brian Logan offered advice for young comedians, discussed being spotted at a show, demystified star ratings, and considered whether the fringe is really ‘Edinburgh’ Achhca asks: Hi Brian! Reviews at the fringe seem to have extra weight to them, especially the exact star rating - four stars can go on the poster, three stars may as well be zero. What are your criteria for stars, and is it informed by the knowledge that a 4+ will end up stapled on posters across the city? And brion asks: Why have you offered so few five star reviews? What is your rubric for a five star score? Brian: I try to think about star ratings as little as possible. My job, as I see it, is to write something insightful, respectful and hopefully entertaining about a show; and to express all I have to say about that show in words. At a stretch, I recognise the usefulness, to some, of then appending a star rating to that review. But I wish we didn’t have to. It’s reductive and dumb. My own kids ask me after I’ve seen a show ‘what did you give it?’ rather than ‘what did you think of it?’ That makes me sad. But: let’s not take ourselves too seriously! There was once, reputedly, a critic who never gave three-star reviews because he knew no one would read them. But most shows are three-star shows – i.e. good, enjoyable, competent if unexceptional. I’ll try to err on the side of enthusiasm whenever I can. God knows my own work has received enough two- (and lower) star reviews over the years. I know how depressing that is. Matter to whom? They matter to me. My experience of art (books, movies, TV, whatever) is so massively enriched and improved by cross-referring it with the experience of reviewers. As soon as I close the last page of a book, I jump online and read what other people have said about it. I love to read what cleverer or better informed or just different minds to my own think about the shows and paintings and songs that I’ve experienced too. I find it weird that anyone might think otherwise. Whether reviews matter in terms of an artwork’s success or failure (and who gets to define that?!) is less clear. Depends on the show. Depends on the circumstances. At any rate, reviewers are part of an ecology that responds to the art and entertainment that gets put out into the world, and one of the many factors that may influence how those artworks are received, understood and savoured. And the world would be more drab and undistinguished without them. (But then, I would say that…) Continue reading...

threads_text:
《衛報》開放讀者提問英國演員伊美黛．史丹頓（Imelda Staunton），她的角色橫跨《落跑雞》裡的邦蒂、《王冠》裡的伊麗莎白二世、《哈利波特》系列裡令人生畏的恩不里居教授，也是《柏靈頓熊》三部曲裡露西阿姨的配音演員。同一天，《衛報》喜劇線記者布萊恩．羅根公開回覆讀者對愛丁堡藝穗節喜劇評論的提問。他坦言自己盡量不去想星級評分這件事，覺得這種制度有點粗暴，但也理解讀者需要一個簡單的參考值；對於「喜劇圈被左派意識形態把持」的說法，他直言這是無稽之談。

本則整理自 The Guardian 於 2026 年 8 月 4 日發佈的報導。
voice_text: 《衛報》這邊，開放讀者提問英國演員伊美黛．史丹頓。她演過《王冠》裡的伊麗莎白二世，也演過《哈利波特》系列裡令人生畏的恩不里居教授，還替《柏靈頓熊》系列的露西阿姨配音。同一天，《衛報》的喜劇線記者也公開回覆了讀者對愛丁堡藝穗節喜劇評論的提問。他說，自己盡量不去想星級評分，這套制度有點粗暴。對於「喜劇圈被左派意識形態把持」的說法，他覺得是無稽之談。
